title: Jensen Huang's brief Nvidia exile exposed a weakness in the AI boom
excerpt: AI is supposed to be an inevitable revolution. Jensen Huang's brief exile from Nvidia revealed just how much the industry's future hinges on him.
content_html:
So the AI bubble is just one guy?

The future of AI is supposedly inevitable. So why did Jensen Huang's ouster nearly derail the whole thing?

By Emily Stewart

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-24T10:18:01.292Z

The bull case around AI generally goes something like this: The technology is amazingly transformative and will inevitably upend the global economy. There's no stopping the AI train. In the optimistic view, this means machines will do all the grunt work, freeing people up to pursue their passions. In the pessimistic view, humanity is wiped out. They're two sides of the same future-cast coin.

The events unfolding around AI in recent weeks, however, suggest a different reality. Former-and-current-again Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's ouster ignited industry-wide panic and a market sell-off. Even the White House got involved. Nvidia's board reinstated him, and the market subsequently rallied. With Jensen and his leather jacket back in the driver's seat, all in AI land is allegedly well. Or is it?

It's not exactly heartening that the supposedly predestined future of everything could hinge on the employment status of one guy.

Huang's brief exile reveals how much of the current AI boom is not a force of technological destiny but instead a sprawling, expensive, fragile business bet. Nvidia has made itself into a central source of capital, confidence, and coordination for the industry. Huang has positioned himself as its chief salesman, dealmaker, and prophet. His return may have reassured investors that the show can go on for now, but the episode remains unsettling.

"A lot of it has been about hype, and Jensen's been one of the best hypesters. You take that hype away, and you start looking at the cold, hard facts, and stuff doesn't make that much sense," says Gary Marcus, an AI researcher and longtime skeptic of some of the industry's grandest claims. "The industry still has not shown that it can actually be profitable and financially sound in the long term."

This latest round of AI anxiety didn't begin with Huang's ouster. Stocks connected to the AI trade had already been sliding for weeks as investors fretted over whether all of this spending on chips, data centers, and electricity could generate the returns boosters promised. Huang's departure was a "headline accelerant," says Luke Lango, a tech analyst at InvestorPlace.

A lot of it has been about hype, and Jensen's been one of the best hypesters.

One reason is that Nvidia isn't an ordinary supplier — it doesn't just make the chips and ship them out. Under Huang, the company became a venture investor and capital backer to the AI ecosystem, crafting a complex circular financing mechanism that underpins the sector. (In the simplest terms, it invests in AI startups that turn around and buy its chips.) Nvidia is the "central bank for artificial intelligence," Lango says. After Huang's decision to step down, investors worried that different leadership — say, that of chief financial officer and interim CEO Colette Kress — might make that bank a little more choosy.

That doesn't necessarily mean that Huang's value is only in financial engineering. The semiconductor industry is "brutal," says Andy Wu, an associate professor of business administration at Harvard Business School, and it doesn't take a lot of screw-ups to fall behind. Nvidia's current success is the payoff from bets Huang made 20 years ago, and he's still looking ahead, making "serious investments" in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and 3D graphics. "Success in all of those new areas is important for justifying Nvidia's valuation," Wu says. In his view, investors and employees don't give hired CEOs as much latitude to make audacious gambles as they do executives who have been there from the beginning. Our modern age is, after all, in the thrall of the cult of the founder.

How financially sound is all of this, especially if one man's indiscretions threaten to pop the entire bubble?

"Nvidia is a remarkably important and remarkably complex company, and there are few humans on this earth capable of and interested in being CEO of that particular company," Wu says.

Huang's return has calmed markets for now, but the drama has highlighted one of the main questions underpinning the AI boom: How financially sound is all of this, especially if one man's indiscretions threaten to pop the entire bubble?

It can simultaneously be the case that there is "tremendous potential" for value creation from AI and a "serious short-term problem" in capturing that value in the form of increased productivity or corporate financial gains, Wu says. Many of the companies at the forefront of developing AI may not end up in a good position to reap big returns from it, even if the technology they champion genuinely reshapes how we work and live. Some of the biggest names in the business, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, aren't yet profitable. They're investing and borrowing a lot of money while on what they hope will ultimately be a lucrative path. There are no guarantees on how that will work out.

"Bringing Huang back will get a lot of people excited, but it won't, in my view, change the fundamentals, which is that Nvidia's customers are not making a lot of money with Nvidia's chips," Marcus says.

AI faces a lot of headwinds. Financing is growing tighter as lenders and investors get more antsy about return timelines and massive capital outlays. Supply chains remain tight. Companies are questioning whether they're deriving value from using the tech, and economic data shows no sign of a massive productivity boon. There's plenty of reason to suspect this technology may not be as revolutionary as its loudest proponents suggest. Public sentiment on data centers specifically, and AI more broadly, is increasingly negative. President Donald Trump's involvement in the goings-on at Nvidia is likely to lead to more public and political scrutiny of the sector.

"When you make a public show of the most visible person in AI being ostensibly untouchable, you really piss off the public," Lango says. "Not the Silicon Valley crowd, the Main Street crowd."

Much of that Main Street crowd is now looking at Jensen Huang and Nvidia, wondering how so much of their technological, financial, and even existential future is seemingly wrapped up in a single guy. If an industry really is healthy, one person should not matter this much. Father Time comes for us all — or, you know, an alleged Chinese spy.

Emily Stewart is a senior correspondent at Business Insider, writing about business and the economy.

blocks.html_en: Emily Stewart is a senior correspondent on Business Insider’s Discourse team. She focuses on consumerism, culture, and the economy, among other topics. Some of her biggest stories have explored Red Lobster’s demise, middle-class shoplifting, convenience stores’ struggles, the rise of illicit drugs as work performance-enhancers, and generational finance trends, including Gen Z’s love for AmEx and the impending avalanche of baby boomers’ stuff. She also writes regularly about sports betting, event ticketing, the alcohol industry, work, millennials, and economic trends. Emily appears regularly on nationally syndicated radio shows and podcasts, including Marketplace, The Weekend Dive, and Today, Explained. She has guest hosted C-SPAN’s “After Words” and moderated multiple panels on economic policy and workplace dynamics.Before joining Business Insider, Emily was at Vox, where she covered business and the economy and wrote a newsletter, “The Big Squeeze,” about how people experience the forces of the economy and capitalism day to day. Prior to that, she worked at TheStreet.

content_html_zh:
So the AI bubble is just one guy?

The future of AI is supposedly inevitable. So why did Jensen Huang's ouster nearly derail the whole thing?

作者：Emily Stewart 您目前正在关注该作者！ Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-24T10:18:01.292Z

The bull case around AI generally goes something like this: The technology is amazingly transformative and will inevitably upend the global economy. There's no stopping the AI train. In the optimistic view, this means machines will do all the grunt work, freeing people up to pursue their passions. In the pessimistic view, humanity is wiped out. They're two sides of the same future-cast coin.

The events unfolding around AI in recent weeks, however, suggest a different reality. Former-and-current-again Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's ouster ignited industry-wide panic and a market sell-off. Even the White House got involved. Nvidia's board reinstated him, and the market subsequently rallied. With Jensen and his leather jacket back in the driver's seat, all in AI land is allegedly well. 或者是吗？

It's not exactly heartening that the supposedly predestined future of everything could hinge on the employment status of one guy.

Huang's brief exile reveals how much of the current AI boom is not a force of technological destiny but instead a sprawling, expensive, fragile business bet. Nvidia has made itself into a central source of capital, confidence, and coordination for the industry. Huang has positioned himself as its chief salesman, dealmaker, and prophet. His return may have reassured investors that the show can go on for now, but the episode remains unsettling.

"A lot of it has been about hype, and Jensen's been one of the best hypesters. You take that hype away, and you start looking at the cold, hard facts, and stuff doesn't make that much sense," says Gary Marcus, an AI researcher and longtime skeptic of some of the industry's grandest claims. "The industry still has not shown that it can actually be profitable and financially sound in the long term."

This latest round of AI anxiety didn't begin with Huang's ouster. Stocks connected to the AI trade had already been sliding for weeks as investors fretted over whether all of this spending on chips, data centers, and electricity could generate the returns boosters promised. Huang's departure was a "headline accelerant," says Luke Lango, a tech analyst at InvestorPlace.

A lot of it has been about hype, and Jensen's been one of the best hypesters.

One reason is that Nvidia isn't an ordinary supplier — it doesn't just make the chips and ship them out. Under Huang, the company became a venture investor and capital backer to the AI ecosystem, crafting a complex circular financing mechanism that underpins the sector. (In the simplest terms, it invests in AI startups that turn around and buy its chips.) Nvidia is the "central bank for artificial intelligence," Lango says. After Huang's decision to step down, investors worried that different leadership — say, that of chief financial officer and interim CEO Colette Kress — might make that bank a little more choosy.

That doesn't necessarily mean that Huang's value is only in financial engineering. The semiconductor industry is "brutal," says Andy Wu, an associate professor of business administration at Harvard Business School, and it doesn't take a lot of screw-ups to fall behind. Nvidia's current success is the payoff from bets Huang made 20 years ago, and he's still looking ahead, making "serious investments" in autonomous vehicles, robotics, and 3D graphics. "Success in all of those new areas is important for justifying Nvidia's valuation," Wu says. In his view, investors and employees don't give hired CEOs as much latitude to make audacious gambles as they do executives who have been there from the beginning. Our modern age is, after all, in the thrall of the cult of the founder.

How financially sound is all of this, especially if one man's indiscretions threaten to pop the entire bubble?

"Nvidia is a remarkably important and remarkably complex company, and there are few humans on this earth capable of and interested in being CEO of that particular company," Wu says.

Huang's return has calmed markets for now, but the drama has highlighted one of the main questions underpinning the AI boom: How financially sound is all of this, especially if one man's indiscretions threaten to pop the entire bubble?

It can simultaneously be the case that there is "tremendous potential" for value creation from AI and a "serious short-term problem" in capturing that value in the form of increased productivity or corporate financial gains, Wu says. Many of the companies at the forefront of developing AI may not end up in a good position to reap big returns from it, even if the technology they champion genuinely reshapes how we work and live. Some of the biggest names in the business, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, aren't yet profitable. They're investing and borrowing a lot of money while on what they hope will ultimately be a lucrative path. There are no guarantees on how that will work out.

"Bringing Huang back will get a lot of people excited, but it won't, in my view, change the fundamentals, which is that Nvidia's customers are not making a lot of money with Nvidia's chips," Marcus says.

AI faces a lot of headwinds. Financing is growing tighter as lenders and investors get more antsy about return timelines and massive capital outlays. Supply chains remain tight. Companies are questioning whether they're deriving value from using the tech, and economic data shows no sign of a massive productivity boon. There's plenty of reason to suspect this technology may not be as revolutionary as its loudest proponents suggest. Public sentiment on data centers specifically, and AI more broadly, is increasingly negative. President Donald Trump's involvement in the goings-on at Nvidia is likely to lead to more public and political scrutiny of the sector.

"When you make a public show of the most visible person in AI being ostensibly untouchable, you really piss off the public," Lango says. "Not the Silicon Valley crowd, the Main Street crowd."

Much of that Main Street crowd is now looking at Jensen Huang and Nvidia, wondering how so much of their technological, financial, and even existential future is seemingly wrapped up in a single guy. If an industry really is healthy, one person should not matter this much. Father Time comes for us all — or, you know, an alleged Chinese spy.
